(Note: #12472 and #16626 are already referenced in your issue.)

## Paging interested parties

Tagging folks from related discussions who may find this relevant:

- @ArtyMcLabin — you opened #12472 for native Claude Code hooks compat, this issue narrows the scope to the specific missing primitive: message injection into conversation context
- @yehudacohen — your `session.stopping` work in #16598 / #16626 is the prerequisite for the Stop hook side of this. The `output.inject()` + `output.continue()` API proposed here would build directly on top of that
- @marcusquinn — you offered to validate the aidevops workflow against #16598, the same `output.inject()` pattern would cover your PostToolUse lint-on-edit use case
- @ppiankov — your pastewatch MCP secret enforcement case is a perfect example: `tool.execute.before` can block the tool today, but injecting a message like "use pastewatch_read_file instead" so the AI actually sees it requires this feature
- @gl33mer @parkuman @nagy135 — you've been following the hooks discussion, this adds concrete benchmark data (96.7% vs 6.7%) showing the impact of missing message injection

The core argument: OpenCode's plugin system can already *intercept* tool calls, but skills that need **ongoing behavioral enforcement** (planning, linting, security) degrade severely because there's no way to inject reminders the AI actually sees. Compaction makes it worse — behavioral rules from initial skill loading are the first thing lost.

## 🐱 Gentle nudge to the team

```
    /\_____/\
   /  o   o  \
  ( ==  ^  == )
   )         (
  (           )
 ( (  )   (  ) )
(__(__)___(__)__)

  "plz... can haz
   output.inject()?"
```

Hey OpenCode team — would love to get some eyes on this from the core maintainers:

- @thdxr — you're assigned to #12472 which covers the broader Claude Code hooks compat. This issue distills the single most impactful missing primitive: letting plugin hooks inject messages into the AI's conversation. The benchmark data (96.7% → ~6.7% without enforcement hooks) makes a strong case. Would love to hear if `output.inject()` on `tool.execute.after` is something that fits the plugin architecture direction.
- @adamdotdevin @nexxeln @Hona — as core team members, curious if this aligns with the plugin system roadmap. The proposed API is minimal (one new method on the output object), but it would unlock an entire category of enforcement-based skills that currently only work on Claude Code.
- @jayair @fwang — you've both been active contributors. The `session.stopping` draft PR (#16598) by @yehudacohen already tackles half of this (the Stop hook side). The other half (PostToolUse message injection) is arguably simpler to implement.
- @kujtimiihoxha — your work on the plugin system internals means you'd know best whether `output.inject()` is feasible within the current hook execution pipeline.

This isn't just about one skill — it's about making OpenCode's skill ecosystem competitive for any workflow that needs the AI to **stay on track** beyond initial instructions. The data shows it's a 10x difference. 🙏

I've been building [opencode-voice](https://github.com/mathew-cf/opencode-voice), a companion tool that adds local push-to-talk dictation (whisper.cpp) to OpenCode. It hits all three gaps directly:

- **Session awareness**: The `use-session-api` branch had to build a heuristic that tracks `session.updated`/`session.created` SSE events and guesses which session is active. It cannot know which session the user is actually viewing.
- **Input injection**: The `main` branch uses `/tui/append-prompt` which silently does nothing in web mode. The `use-session-api` branch switched to the session API but lost the ability to stage text for user review before sending.
- **Shutdown**: The tool has to call `std::process::exit(0)` because the global hotkey listener thread cannot be gracefully cancelled, and there's no OpenCode shutdown event to trigger cleanup.

The entire project exists as a separate process rather than a plugin because the plugin API doesn't have the primitives needed.

After reading the docs, I think I may have identified the potential issue affecting me:

- `timeout` controls the **total request duration**
- `chunkTimeout` controls the **delay between each SSE chunk** — if no chunk arrives within that window, the connection is dropped

Local models are slow to generate, so chunks arrive with long gaps between them. The default `chunkTimeout` is too short and kills the connection before the model finishes.

**Fix:** add `chunkTimeout` to your provider `options` in your global config file.

### Config file location

| OS | Path |
|---|---|
| **Linux / Debian / Ubuntu** | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` |
| **macOS** | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` |
| **Windows** | `%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\opencode.json` |
| **Windows (older installs)** | `%APPDATA%\opencode\opencode.json` |

> On Windows you can open the Run dialog (`WIN+R`) and paste the path directly.

### Config

```json
"options": {
  "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1",
  "timeout": 1200000,
  "chunkTimeout": 600000
}
```

- `timeout: 1200000` = 20 minutes total request duration
- `chunkTimeout: 600000` = 10 minutes between each SSE chunk

Adjust values based on your model's generation speed.

I've narrowed it down to something happening when the web app tries to open a connection to the terminal https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/f2d3a4c70f6e9c5e233e1a47c55bb068639fd821/packages/app/src/components/terminal.tsx#L512-L521 Basically, when the websocket tries to open, it does not contain the Basic Authorization header, causing a 401 which then causes the browser to clear its existing Basic Auth from memory and request a new one. Repro Steps - open opencode in a private/incognito window - type in username password - open any project - open the terminal (this causes the 401 loop) Workaround, set the username password in the server settings (on top of the basic auth request). I honestly didn't even know this was a thing... I'll ask OpenCode to post the findings on my research here in a moment

## Root Cause Analysis

The infinite authentication loop is caused by the terminal's WebSocket connection explicitly sending wrong credentials, which poisons the browser's HTTP Basic Auth cache.

### The Bug

When the web app opens a terminal, `terminal.tsx` constructs a WebSocket URL with explicit credentials:

```typescript
// packages/app/src/components/terminal.tsx (current)
url.username = server.current?.http.username ?? "opencode"
url.password = server.current?.http.password ?? ""
```

For **web browser access** (not desktop), `server.current.http` has no stored `username` or `password` — the user authenticated via the browser's native Basic Auth dialog, and those credentials are never captured by the app. So this evaluates to:

- `url.username = "opencode"`
- `url.password = ""` (empty string)

The WebSocket URL becomes `ws://opencode:@host:port/pty/.../connect`, which explicitly tells the browser to send `Authorization: Basic b3BlbmNvZGU6` (base64 of `opencode:`) — overriding the browser's cached (correct) Basic Auth credentials.

The server rejects this (empty password ≠ real password) with **401 Unauthorized**. This 401 on the WebSocket handshake poisons the browser's auth cache for the entire origin, causing all subsequent requests to fail and triggering the infinite re-authentication loop.

### Why regular HTTP requests work

The PUT request to create the PTY (`PUT /pty/{id}`) works fine because it uses the SDK's `fetch()`, which inherits the browser's cached Basic Auth credentials automatically. Only the WebSocket is broken because it explicitly overrides credentials via the URL.

### Regression History

**PR #13813** (`1bb857417`, Feb 18) introduced the latent bug by removing a conditional guard:

```diff
-// BEFORE: Only set WebSocket creds when desktop app provides them
-if (window.__OPENCODE__?.serverPassword) {
-  url.username = "opencode"
-  url.password = window.__OPENCODE__?.serverPassword
-}

+// AFTER: Always sets creds unconditionally — empty for web browser
+url.username = server.current?.http.username ?? ""
+url.password = server.current?.http.password ?? ""
```

Before this change, the web browser path left the WebSocket URL without explicit credentials, so the browser's auth cache handled authentication correctly.

**PR #17061** (`c9c0318e0`, Mar 12) then turned this latent bug into an active one by changing the username fallback from `""` to `"opencode"`. With both username and password as empty strings, some browsers treat the URL as having no credentials and still use the auth cache. With `username="opencode"` and `password=""`, the browser now explicitly sends wrong credentials, guaranteeing the 401.

### Suggested Fix

Only set explicit WebSocket credentials when the server connection actually has stored credentials (i.e., the user entered them in the app's "Add Server" dialog, not via the browser's native auth prompt):

```typescript
if (server.current?.http.password) {
  url.username = server.current.http.username ?? "opencode"
  url.password = server.current.http.password
}
```

This lets the browser's Basic Auth cache handle WebSocket authentication transparently for web browser users — the same way it already works for all regular HTTP requests (PUT, GET, SSE, etc.).

Why would this ticket require additional code? SSE is a standard protocol for server communication.
SSE also naturally lends itself to the iterative semi-streaming similarity to `opencode run` with `--format json`.
When using `opencode run` the message parts are streamed back to the user as completed.
The same could be provided through the `opencode serve` rather than dumping all message parts in one final response.
Applying SSE principals would make robust server connection health during long calculations which exceed short timeout.

We will consider the conclusion: OpenCode does not support SSE or event-driven responses from its serve functionality.
This is a major conclusion, and conflicts with the partial endpoints provided in the OpenCode documentation.  
We are not blocked by this limitation.

Thanks.

We confirmed this looks like a real bug: if assistant text streams live and the run is interrupted before `text-end`, a connected client can have partial text in memory while a reconnecting client reloads an empty persisted text part from SQLite.

I added a red regression test and then a provisional fix that flushes any in-progress assistant text during session finalization, so reconnecting clients see the same partial reply that live clients already saw.

- `bun typecheck`
